title: Why does SA keep running out of water, and where does the pipe money go?

scenes.label: of water lost
lines: Forty seven percent.
That is how much treated water South Africa loses, on the latest government result. Nearly half.
It leaks out of pipes, gets stolen, or is never paid for because of faulty meters.
In June, some Joburg suburbs were still dry twelve days after maintenance work began.
So why does the water keep running out? Where does the pipe money go? And what can you do? Let's open the case.

lines: Meet Gogo Nomsa. She is an example, not a real person.
She lives in Johannesburg. Some mornings she turns on the tap and nothing comes out.
So she carries buckets from a neighbour, and she waits.
Meanwhile, a broken pipe down her street pours clean water into the gutter for days.

items.label: litres lost a day in Joburg

lines: Let's start with the numbers.
The latest government report says nearly half of all treated water is lost. That is forty seven percent.
Lost means leaks, theft, meters that read wrong, and water that nobody pays for.
Reuters says Joburg loses more than a third of its water through burst pipes, about six hundred and fifty five million litres a day.
That is about two hundred and sixty Olympic swimming pools, every single day.
Cape Town does better, at about twenty four percent, the lowest of the big cities, though that counts all unbilled water, not only leaks.
Is this new? No.
A 2013 study of one hundred and thirty two municipalities, which are your local councils, found about thirty seven percent of water was lost.
The minister at the time set a target of fifteen percent.
In 2024, Daily Maverick reported that the losses were getting worse, at about forty seven percent.
And the latest government result is forty seven percent again.
The numbers are counted a little differently, but neither one is close to fifteen.
It is not all bad news, so let's be fair.
Government released its water report cards on thirty first March this year.
For drinking water, things are a little better, and the systems in real danger fell to about eight percent.
But sewage, the dirty water we flush away, is getting worse, with critical systems up from thirty nine to forty seven percent.
The department says drinking water has settled, but at a high level of risk.

Many are asking: why is my tap dry, when water runs down my street?
And: where did the money for fixing pipes go?
Parliament's water committee said new laws are not enough without trained people to do the work.

lines: So why does this keep happening? There are three main suspects.
Old pipes. No upkeep. And where the money goes.

scenes.headline: Pipes replaced in Joburg
lines: Suspect one: old pipes.
Large parts of Joburg's pipes are about eighty years old.
Joburg Water says about sixty percent of its water equipment is past its designed life, like a taxi that should have retired years ago.
The city has about twelve thousand kilometres of pipes, about nine trips from Joburg to Cape Town.
Joburg Water said it must replace between one hundred and seventy five and one hundred and eighty five kilometres a year, but last year it replaced seventeen.
Africa Check says cities should replace about one and a half to two percent of their pipes every year.
And from July to mid December 2025, one Gauteng dashboard recorded more than twenty thousand leaks and bursts.

scenes.headline: Joburg's repair spending
lines: Suspect two: no upkeep, which means fixing leaks and servicing pipes on time, like servicing a car.
In the 2020 and 2021 year, Joburg spent two point eight billion rand on repairs and maintenance.
By 2023 and 2024, that fell to two hundred and twenty nine million, about ninety two percent less.
Treasury says big cities should spend eight percent of their budget on this.
The Auditor-General, who checks how government spends our money, found Joburg spent the least of all eight big cities.
Across the country, thirty one of one hundred and fifty four water councils had no plan to maintain their water systems.

scenes.headline: Joburg's water money

delivered.label: Set aside for pipes and plants

lines: Now the big question: where does the pipe money go?
In February, the Finance Minister said Joburg's water brings in eleven point nine billion rand.
But only one point three billion was set aside for Joburg Water to build and fix things.
Some of that income pays running costs, like buying water from Rand Water.
Even so, many people ask: so where did the rest go?
Some point to four billion rand the city moved out of Joburg Water's account.
The Auditor-General's office says that money exists on paper, not as cash, and both the city and Joburg Water say it is owed.
Another reason: the head of the water department said no law forces councils to spend water income on water pipes.
The audit also found the city overspent by two point three eight billion rand, mainly on staff costs and short-term loan costs.
Unpaid contractors are part of it too, with twenty two water projects delayed over seventy two million rand owed.
Joburg Water also blames theft, vandalism, illegal connections and non-payment, and the city says power cuts hurt pumping.
As for corruption, we found no official finding about Joburg Water, but the city must still explain where the money went.
The Auditor-General reported on every council's books in June.
Poor care of pipes and equipment cost about fifteen billion rand in lost water in one year.
Joburg Water alone lost about ten billion rand of drinking water over four years.
The Auditor-General looked at one hundred and twenty nine building projects and found problems in one hundred and one of them.
The real losses are likely higher, because seventeen councils did not report theirs.
And all eight big cities failed to get a clean audit, which is the top mark.

scenes.headline: Water grants handed back
lines: There is one more twist: some money was given for water, and never spent.
When a council does not spend a grant on time, it has to hand the money back.
North West handed back about three hundred and nine million rand in water grants.
Eastern Cape returned about two hundred and sixty one million rand.
And Free State sent back about two hundred and thirty four million rand.

scenes.headline: The short answer
points: Old pipes are not replaced fast
lines: So, what is the short answer?
Pipes are old, and Joburg replaced seventeen kilometres when it needed well over a hundred.
Repair spending fell sharply, so leaks run for days.
And no law forces councils to spend water income on water, so the money can go elsewhere.

scenes.headline: How to report a leak

steps.title: Note where the leak is
steps.sub: Street name, nearest corner, and a photo

steps.title: Report it to your municipality
steps.sub: Call or use the app, get a reference number

steps.title: Follow up with that number
steps.sub: Keep a record of dates and replies

steps.title: Tell your ward councillor
steps.sub: Ask when the repair will be done

lines: Now, what can you do?
First, note exactly where the leak is, and take a photo.
Second, report it to your municipality and keep the reference number.
Third, follow up using that number, and write down every reply.
And fourth, tell your ward councillor and ask for a date.

items.title: Store some emergency water
items.sub: A few clean containers for dry days

items.title: Check your own taps and meter
items.sub: A moving meter with taps off means a leak

items.title: Ask where water income goes
items.sub: Ask council for the water budget in writing

items.title: Organise your street or ward
items.sub: Report together and attend ward meetings

lines: Keep a few clean containers of water at home for dry days.
Check your own meter, because if it moves with every tap off, you have a leak.
Ask your council in writing where the water income goes.
And organise with neighbours, because a whole street reporting together is harder to ignore.
